beats.say: Here is our series: 64, 81, 100, 121, and it keeps going. One of the four choices does not belong to it. Let's find the odd one out.
First we need the rule. What kind of numbers are these? Think about 8 times 8.

ask.ifNot: Look again. 8 times 8 is 64, and 9 times 9 is 81. Each one is a number multiplied by itself.

beats.say: 8 times 8 is 64. 9 times 9 is 81. Then 10 times 10, and 11 times 11. These are the square numbers, in order.
So a number belongs only if it is some number times itself. Let's test the choices. 13 times 13 is 169, and 15 times 15 is 225.
17 times 17 is 289. So those three all belong. That leaves 176, but let's prove it.
176 is a little more than 169, which is 13 times 13. What is the very next square number after that?

ask.ifNot: The next square after 13 times 13 is 14 times 14, and that is 196.

beats.say: 13 times 13 is 169 and 14 times 14 is 196. 176 sits between them, and there is no whole number between 13 and 14. So 176 is not a square.
So the number that is not in the series is 176.
When a list looks odd, ask what family the numbers belong to. Then test each choice against that family.
Our series starts 24, 39, 53, 66, 78. We want the 10th term, so first we must find the rule.
Look at the jumps between neighbours. They are 15, then 14, then 13, then 12.
The jumps are not the same. So what is happening to them?

ask.ifNot: Read the jumps again: 15, 14, 13, 12. Each one is 1 less than the one before.

beats.say: So the next jumps are 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. Count carefully: 78 is the 5th term, so we need 5 more jumps to reach the 10th.
The 6th term is 78 plus 11, which is 89. The 7th is 89 plus 10, which is 99.
The 8th is 99 plus 9, which is 108. Don't stop there! The 9th is 108 plus 8, which is 116.
One jump is left. Which jump takes us from the 9th term to the 10th?

ask.ifNot: The jumps we listed were 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. We have used four of them, so the last one is 7.

beats.say: 116 plus 7 is 123. So the 10th term is 123.
When the jumps change, find how they change. Then walk forward one term at a time, and keep count of which term you are on.
We must add the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, all the way up to 27. And look, the choices are written as squares. That is a clue.
Let's start small and hunt for a pattern. 1 plus 3 is 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.
Now three odd numbers. 1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9. And 9 is 3 times 3.
Two odd numbers gave 2 times 2. Three gave 3 times 3. What will the first four odd numbers add up to?

ask.ifNot: Follow the pattern. Two numbers gave 2 times 2, and three gave 3 times 3. So four give 4 times 4, which is 16.

beats.say: Yes: 1 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 16. So the sum is always the count of odd numbers, multiplied by itself.
So all we need is the count. Careful, this is the trap: the count is not 27. How many odd numbers are there from 1 to 27?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns. Up to 27 there are 14 odd numbers and 13 even ones.

beats.say: Here is a quick way to count them. Add 1 to the last odd number, then halve. 27 plus 1 is 28, and half of 28 is 14.
There are 14 odd numbers, so the sum is 14 times 14. That is 14 squared.
Remember this lovely fact. Add up the odd numbers starting from 1, and you always get the count times itself.
We are walking backwards from 726, stepping only on odd numbers. We want the 59th one we land on.
Let's begin at the beginning. What is the 1st odd number before 726?

ask.ifNot: Before means smaller. One step down from 726 is 725, and 725 is odd.

beats.say: So 725 is the 1st. Then 723 is the 2nd, and 721 is the 3rd. Each jump back is 2.
From the 1st odd number to the 59th, how many jumps of 2 do we make?

ask.ifNot: From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. So to the 59th it is 1 fewer than 59.

beats.say: That is the trap. 725 is already the 1st, so we need only 58 jumps. And 58 jumps of 2 make 116.
Now go back 116 from 725. Take away 100 to get 625. Then take away 16 more to get 609.
So the 59th odd number before 726 is 609.
Quick check. 609 ends in 9, so it is odd, just as it must be. An even answer could never be right here.
When you count along a list, the jumps are always 1 fewer than the place number. Keep that in your pocket.
This one has three small jobs hidden inside. Find the greatest 2-digit prime. Find two even numbers after it. Then add them.

board.text: 7th + 11th even numbers after the greatest 2-digit prime

beats.say: A prime number has no factors except 1 and itself. Which is the greatest 2-digit prime?

ask.ifNot: 99 is 9 times 11, and 98 is even. So neither is prime. 97 has no factors like that.

beats.say: 99 is 9 times 11. 98 is even, so 2 goes into it. That makes 97 the greatest 2-digit prime.
The 1st even number after 97 is 98. The 2nd is 100. Each jump is 2.
From the 1st even number to the 7th, how many jumps of 2 do we make?

ask.ifNot: The 1st one needs no jump at all. So to reach the 7th we make 6 jumps.

beats.say: 6 jumps of 2 make 12, and 98 plus 12 is 110. So the 7th even number is 110.
For the 11th we make 10 jumps. 10 twos are 20, and 98 plus 20 is 118.
Now add the two numbers. 110 plus 118 is 228.
Look at the choices. 228 is not there! Don't bend your working to fit a choice. When your careful answer is not listed, pick none of these.

board.text: 228 is not listed: None of these

beats.say: Break a long question into small jobs and do them one at a time. And trust your careful working.
Our series is 122, 117, 107, 92, 72, and then a letter A. A stands for the next number, and we must find it.
The numbers are getting smaller. Let's see how much they drop each time. The drops are 5, then 10, then 15, then 20.
The drops are not the same. So what is the next drop?

ask.ifNot: Look at the drops: 5, 10, 15, 20. Each drop is 5 bigger than the last. So after 20 comes 25.

beats.say: The drops grow by 5 each time, so the next drop is 25. This is the trap: don't just take away 20 again.
72 take away 25. First take away 20 to get 52. Then take away 5 more to get 47.
So A is 47.
Check the whole chain of drops: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. It grows steadily, so 47 fits.
When the jumps are not all the same, look at the jumps themselves. They often have a little pattern of their own.
Our series starts 13, 15, 18, 23, 30, 41. We want the 12th term. First, the rule.
Look at the jumps between neighbours. They are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
Those jumps belong to a famous family of numbers. Which one?

ask.ifNot: They are not the odd numbers, because 2 is there and 9 is missing. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 are the prime numbers in order.

beats.say: So each jump is the next prime. Now the trap: to go from the 1st term to the 12th we make 11 jumps, not 12.
So we need the first 11 primes. After 11 come 13, 17, 19, 23, 29 and 31.
Let's add them in friendly groups. The first five make 28. Then 13 and 17 make 30.
19 and 23 make 42. 29 and 31 make 60. All together, 28 plus 30 plus 42 plus 60 is 160.
The 11 jumps add up to 160. Where do we add them on?

ask.ifNot: All 11 jumps were counted from the very start. So they are added to the 1st term, 13.

beats.say: 13 plus 160 is 173. So the 12th term is 173.
When jumps look strange, ask which family they belong to. And remember: reaching the 12th term takes only 11 jumps.
W is a mystery number. We are told that W plus 9 is odd, and we want the 48th even number after it.
If W plus 9 is odd, what kind of number is the very next one, W plus 10?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns. Straight after an odd number comes an even one.

beats.say: So W plus 10 is the 1st even number after it. The 2nd is W plus 12. Each jump is 2.
From the 1st even number to the 48th, how many jumps of 2 do we make?

ask.ifNot: The 1st one needs no jump. From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump, to the 3rd is 2 jumps. So to the 48th it is 47.

beats.say: This is the trap. W plus 10 is already the 1st, so we make only 47 jumps. 47 twos are 94.
We started at W plus 10 and moved 94 further on. 10 plus 94 is 104.
So the 48th even number is W plus 104.
Quick check. W plus 10 is even, and we added 94, which is even. Even plus even stays even. Good.
Even with a letter in it, the idea is the same. Find the 1st one, count 1 fewer jump than the place number, and step on.
Our series starts 24, 41, 58, 75, 92, and keeps going. We want the 28th term. That is a long way along!
First find the jump. 41 minus 24 is 17, and 58 minus 41 is 17 too. So each term is 17 more than the one before.
We could keep going one step at a time, but that is slow. From the 1st term to the 28th, how many jumps do we make?

ask.ifNot: From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the place number.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The 1st term is there before any jump. So we make 1 fewer jump than 28. That is 27 jumps.
27 jumps of 17 is a big sum, so split it. 20 times 17 is 340, and 7 times 17 is 119.
340 plus 119 makes 459. So 27 jumps of 17 cover 459.
The jumps cover 459. What do we do with the 459?

ask.ifNot: The jumps start at the 1st term, which is 24. So the 459 is added on to 24.

beats.say: 24 plus 459 is 483. So the 28th term is 483.
Test the idea on the 5th term, which we can see. 4 jumps of 17 make 68, and 24 plus 68 is 92. It matches.
For a term far along: find the jump, make 1 fewer jump than the term number, multiply, then add the 1st term.
Here x is a mystery number, and x plus 9 is a 2-digit prime. We want the 12th even number after it.
We don't know which prime it is. But we can still say something. Is a 2-digit prime odd or even?

ask.ifNot: An even number has 2 as a factor. The only even prime is 2 itself, and that has just 1 digit.

beats.say: So x plus 9 is odd. That makes x plus 10 the 1st even number after it, and x plus 12 the 2nd. Each jump is 2.
From the 1st even number to the 12th, how many jumps of 2 do we make?

ask.ifNot: The 1st one needs no jump. So the jumps are 1 fewer than 12, which is 11.

beats.say: Careful, that is the trap. x plus 10 is already the 1st, so we make 11 jumps. 11 twos are 22.
We started at x plus 10 and moved 22 further on. 10 plus 22 is 32.
So the 12th even number is x plus 32.
Quick check. x plus 10 is even, and 22 is even. Even plus even stays even, so x plus 32 is an even number. Good.
So the plan is: find the 1st even number, count 1 fewer jump than the place number, and step on in 2s.
The series goes 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, and on. We want the 11th number in it.
First find the jump. 10 minus 7 is 3, and 13 minus 10 is 3 too. So each number is 3 more than the one before.
We could keep going one step at a time, but that is slow. From the 1st number to the 11th, how many jumps do we make?

ask.ifNot: From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the place number.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The 1st number is there before any jump. So we make 1 fewer jump than 11. That is 10 jumps.
10 jumps of 3. 10 times 3 is 30.
The jumps cover 30. What do we do with the 30?

ask.ifNot: The jumps start at the 1st number, which is 7. So the 30 is added on to 7.

beats.say: 7 plus 30 is 37. So the 11th number is 37.
Test the idea on the 5th number, which we can see. 4 jumps of 3 make 12, and 7 plus 12 is 19. It matches.
So remember: the 11th number is only 10 jumps from the 1st. Count the jumps, not the numbers.
The series starts 12, 23, 33, 42, 50. We want the 9th number, so first we need the rule.
Look at the jumps. From 12 to 23 is 11. Then the jumps are 10, then 9, then 8.
So is this a pattern where we add the same amount each time?

ask.ifNot: Read the jumps again: 11, 10, 9, 8. They shrink by 1 each time.

beats.say: The jumps shrink by 1. So the next ones are 7, 6, 5 and 4. And 50 is the 5th number, so 4 more jumps reach the 9th.
The 6th number is 50 plus 7, which is 57. The 7th is 57 plus 6, which is 63.
The 8th number is 63 plus 5, which is 68. One more jump to go.
Which jump takes us from the 8th number to the 9th?

ask.ifNot: The jumps after 50 are 7, 6, 5 and 4. We have used three of them, so the last one is 4.

beats.say: 68 plus 4 is 72. So the 9th number is 72.
When the jumps change, find how they change. Then step forward, and name each number as you go so you stop at the right one.
We need to add the first 12 odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, and so on. Adding 12 numbers is slow, so let's hunt for a short cut.

board.text: Sum of the first 12 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: Start small. The first 2 odd numbers are 1 and 3. They add to 4, and 4 is 2 times 2.
The first 3 odd numbers are 1, 3 and 5. They add to 9, and 9 is 3 times 3.
Can you see it coming? What do the first 4 odd numbers add up to?

ask.ifNot: 2 odd numbers made 2 times 2. 3 odd numbers made 3 times 3. So 4 odd numbers make 4 times 4, which is 16.

beats.say: Yes: 1 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 16. The sum is always the count, multiplied by itself.
So what is the sum of the first 12 odd numbers?

ask.ifNot: The count is 12, and the rule is the count times itself. So it is 12 times 12.

beats.say: 12 times 12. 12 tens are 120, and 12 twos are 24. Together that makes 144.
So the first 12 odd numbers add up to 144.
Keep this fact. Add the odd numbers starting from 1, and the total is always the count times itself.
Here is the series: 90, 85, 75, 60, 40, and then a question mark. Let's find the number that belongs there.
The numbers go down. From 90 to 85 is a drop of 5. From 85 to 75 is a drop of 10. Then 15, then 20.
Look at those drops: 5, 10, 15, 20. What will the next drop be?

ask.ifNot: Each drop is 5 more than the one before. After 20 comes 25.

beats.say: Careful here. It is tempting to take away 20 again, but the drops keep growing by 5. The next drop is 25.
40 take away 25. Take away 20 first to get 20. Then take away 5 more to get 15.
So the missing number is 15.
Check: the drops now read 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Every drop is 5 bigger than the last, so 15 fits.
So the plan is: find the drops, spot how the drops change, then make the next drop from the last number.
This series begins 12, 19, 26, 33, 40. We need its 38th term, far too far to count one by one.
First find the jump. 19 minus 12 is 7, and 26 minus 19 is 7 too. So each term is 7 more than the one before.
We could keep going one step at a time, but that is slow. From the 1st term to the 38th, how many jumps do we make?

ask.ifNot: From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the place number.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The 1st term is there before any jump. So we make 1 fewer jump than 38. That is 37 jumps.
37 jumps of 7 is a big sum, so split it. 30 times 7 is 210, and 7 times 7 is 49.
210 plus 49 makes 259. So 37 jumps of 7 cover 259.
The jumps cover 259. What do we do with the 259?

ask.ifNot: The jumps start at the 1st term, which is 12. So the 259 is added on to 12.

beats.say: 12 plus 259 is 271. So the 38th term is 271.
Test the idea on the 5th term, which we can see. 4 jumps of 7 make 28, and 12 plus 28 is 40. It matches.
Find the jump, count 1 fewer jump than the term number, multiply, and add the 1st term. That works for any steady pattern.
The series goes 92, 88, 84, 80, 76. It goes down by 4 each time, and we want the 18th term.
First find the jump. 92 minus 88 is 4, and 88 minus 84 is 4 too. So each term is 4 less than the one before.
We could keep going one step at a time, but that is slow. From the 1st term to the 18th, how many jumps do we make?

ask.ifNot: From the 1st to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the place number.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The 1st term is there before any jump. So we make 1 fewer jump than 18. That is 17 jumps.
17 jumps of 4 is a big sum, so split it. 10 times 4 is 40, and 7 times 4 is 28.
40 plus 28 makes 68. So 17 jumps of 4 cover 68.
The jumps cover 68. The numbers are going down, so what do we do with the 68?

ask.ifNot: The jumps start at the 1st term, 92, and they go down. So we take the 68 away from 92.

beats.say: 92 take away 68 is 24. So the 18th term is 24.
Test the idea on the 5th term, which we can see. 4 jumps of 4 make 16, and 92 take away 16 is 76. It matches.
Going down works just like going up. Count 1 fewer jump than the term number, multiply, and take that away from the 1st term.
The sequence is 1, 7, 13, 19, 25, and it carries on until 103. We are not asked for a term. We are asked how many terms there are.
First the jump. 7 minus 1 is 6, and 13 minus 7 is 6 too. Each term is 6 more than the one before.
How far is it from the first term to the last? 103 minus 1 is 102.
That distance of 102 is covered in jumps of 6. How do we find the number of jumps?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 6s fit into 102. That is a division.

beats.say: Split 102 into 60 and 42. 60 divided by 6 is 10. 42 divided by 6 is 7. So there are 17 jumps.
There are 17 jumps. So how many terms are there?

ask.ifNot: Think small. 1 jump joins 2 numbers. 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: Here is the trap. Jumps sit between the terms, and the first term is there before any jump. So we add 1.
Check with the start of the list. From 1 to 25 is 4 jumps, and there are 5 terms. One more than the jumps. So there are 18 terms in all.
To count the terms: find the distance, divide by the jump, then add 1 for the first term.
Five symbols repeat in the same order, again and again: star, square, circle, triangle, circled plus. Which one lands in the 37th place?
We won't draw 37 symbols. Think in groups of 5. The last symbol of each group sits in place 5, then 10, then 15, then 20, and so on.
Which is the last group to finish before the 37th place? It ends at place...

ask.ifNot: 7 groups of 5 end at place 35. The next group would end at 40, which is past 37.

beats.say: 7 full groups use up 35 places. And 37 minus 35 leaves 2 more places.
So the 37th symbol is the same as which symbol in a group?

ask.ifNot: After place 35 a new group starts. One place on is the 1st symbol, and two places on is the 2nd.

beats.say: Place 36 starts a new group with the star. Place 37 comes next, and that is the square.
So the 37th symbol is the square.
Here is the same idea in one line. 37 is 7 fives and 2 more. The 2 left over tells you the place inside the group.
For any repeating pattern: take out the full groups, then count on with what is left over.
What a jumpy pattern! 2, 50, 5, 46, 8, 42, 11, 38. Up, down, up, down. We want the 15th number.
It looks messy, but there is a trick. What do you get if you read only every second number, starting with the 2?

ask.ifNot: Skip one each time: 2, then 5, then 8, then 11. Those go up by 3.

beats.say: Two patterns are woven together. In the odd places: 2, 5, 8, 11, going up by 3. In the even places: 50, 46, 42, 38, going down by 4.
15 is an odd number, so the 15th place is an odd place. Our answer comes from the pattern that goes up by 3.
Here is the trap. The 15th number of the mixed pattern is which number of 2, 5, 8, 11?

ask.ifNot: That pattern uses only every second place: 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on up to 15. Count those places and you get 8.

beats.say: The odd places are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15. That is 8 places. So we want the 8th number of 2, 5, 8, 11.
The 8th number is 7 jumps from the 1st. 7 jumps of 3 make 21.
2 plus 21 is 23. So the 15th number in the pattern is 23.
Check by listing that pattern: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23. The 8th one is 23.
When a pattern zigzags, split it into two. Then work out which of the two your place belongs to.
The pattern 4, 9, 14, 19 goes up by 5 each time and stops at 99. We must count how many of its numbers are even.
Look at the first few. 4 is even. 9 is odd. 14 is even. 19 is odd. They take turns.
Why do they take turns like that?

ask.ifNot: 5 is an odd number. Adding an odd number always changes even to odd, and odd to even.

beats.say: So the even ones are every second number: 4, 14, 24, and so on. They go up by 10 and all end in 4. The last one before 99 is 94.
Now count them. From 4 to 94 is a distance of 90. Each jump is 10, so that is 9 jumps.
There are 9 jumps. So how many even numbers are there?

ask.ifNot: Jumps sit between the numbers. 9 jumps join 10 numbers, because both ends count.

beats.say: Careful with this last step. 9 jumps join 10 numbers. So 10 of the numbers are even.
We can list them to be sure: 4, 14, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, 74, 84, 94. Count them, and there are 10.
So: pick out the numbers you want, see their own pattern, count the jumps, and add 1.
The numbers climb up to 4 and come back down, over and over. We want the 100th number, and we are not going to write 100 numbers!
A repeating pattern is made of one block, copied again and again. So first we must find the block.
Which block is copied again and again?

ask.ifNot: This is the trap. If the block ended in 1, the next block would start with 1 too, and we would see 1, 1. So that 1 starts the next block.

beats.say: The block is 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2. It has 6 numbers, not 7. The next 1 begins a new block.
Now fill up with blocks of 6. 10 blocks use 60 numbers. 6 more blocks use 36. So 16 blocks use 96 numbers.
100 take away 96 leaves 4. So the 100th number is the 4th number of the next block.
What is the 4th number in the block 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2?

ask.ifNot: Count along the block. The 1st is 1, the 2nd is 2, the 3rd is 3 and the 4th is 4.

beats.say: So the 100th number in the pattern is 4.
For a repeating pattern: find the true block, take out the full blocks, and count on with what is left.
A long chain: 20 minus 19, plus 18, minus 17, and so on, down to plus 2, minus 1. We won't work from left to right. There is a smarter way.
Look at the numbers two at a time. 20 minus 19. Then 18 minus 17. Right down to 2 minus 1.
What is each pair worth?

ask.ifNot: 20 minus 19 is 1. 18 minus 17 is 1. Every pair leaves exactly 1.

beats.say: Each pair is worth 1. So the whole chain is just 1 plus 1 plus 1, once for every pair.
There are 20 numbers in the chain. How many pairs do they make?

ask.ifNot: A pair uses up 2 numbers. So 20 numbers make half of 20 pairs, which is 10.

beats.say: That is the step to be careful with. 20 numbers, but only 10 pairs.
10 pairs, each worth 1. So the value of the whole chain is 10.
When a long sum has a rhythm, group it into pairs. Often every pair is worth the same, and the rest is easy.
Farid makes a triangle of dots. Row 1 has 1 dot, row 2 has 2 dots, row 3 has 3, and so on. He has 60 dots. How many will be left over?
Let's keep a running total of the dots he has used. After row 1: 1. After row 2: 3. After row 3: 6. After row 4: 10.
Carry on. Row 5 brings the total to 15. Row 6 makes 21. Row 7 makes 28. Row 8 makes 36.
Row 9 adds 9 dots: 36 plus 9 is 45. Row 10 adds 10 dots: 45 plus 10 is 55.
After 10 rows he has used 55 of his 60 dots. Can he finish row 11?

ask.ifNot: After 10 rows, only 60 take away 55 dots are left. Row 11 needs 11 dots, and that is too many.

beats.say: Row 11 would bring the total to 66. That is more than 60, so he stops after 10 complete rows.
He used 55 dots. 60 take away 55 leaves 5.
Careful with what the question asks. 10 is the number of rows. We were asked for the dots left over, and that is 5.
Keep a running total, stop before you go past the limit, and then subtract.
Arun saves 5 rupees on day 1. Each day after, he saves 3 rupees more than the day before. On which day does his total first go past 100 rupees?

board.text: Total first more than ₹100 on day ?

beats.say: Two different things are growing here. Which one has to go past 100?

choices: the amount saved on one day
ask.ifNot: Read the question again. It asks about the total money he has saved, with all the days added together.

beats.say: Let's make a table. Each day he saves 3 more: 5, 8, 11, 14. And we keep a running total: 5, 13, 24, 38.

spec.note: Add each day's saving to the total

beats.say: Day 5: he saves 17, and the total is 55. Day 6: he saves 20, total 75. Day 7: he saves 23, total 98.
After day 7 the total is 98. Has it gone past 100 yet?

ask.ifNot: 98 is close, but it is still less than 100. More than 100 means past it.

beats.say: On day 8 he saves 26. 98 plus 26 is 124. Now the total is past 100.
So the total first goes past 100 rupees on the 8th day.
When a question is about a total, keep a running total, and stop at the first moment it crosses the line.
Here is the pattern: 2, 6, 4, 12, 10, 30, 28. It jumps up a lot, then drops a little. We want the 10th number.
How do we get from 2 to 6, and then from 6 to 4?

ask.ifNot: Test it further along. 4 times 3 is 12, and 12 take away 2 is 10. Times 3, then take away 2, works every time.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6. 6 take away 2 is 4. 4 times 3 is 12. 12 take away 2 is 10. The two moves take turns.
7 numbers are given. The last move was take away 2, from 30 down to 28. So the next move is times 3.
The 8th number is 28 times 3, which is 84. The 9th is 84 take away 2, which is 82.
What is the move from the 9th number to the 10th?

ask.ifNot: The moves take turns. We just took away 2, so now it is times 3.

beats.say: 82 times 3. 80 threes are 240, and 2 threes are 6. That makes 246.
So the 10th number is 246. Don't stop early: 84 is only the 8th, and 82 is only the 9th.
When a pattern goes up and down, look for two moves that take turns. Then keep careful count of which number you are on.
Two patterns. A goes up in 4s: 5, 9, 13, 17. B goes up in 7s: 2, 9, 16, 23. Both have 9. Where do they meet next?
Start from the 9 they share. A moves on by 4, 8, 12, 16, and so on. B moves on by 7, 14, 21, 28, and so on.
They meet when the distance from 9 is in both lists. What is the first distance that is in both?

ask.ifNot: Look along both lists. 28 is in the 4s list and in the 7s list. It is the first number in both.

beats.say: 4 times 7 is 28. It is the smallest number that both 4 and 7 go into. So the patterns meet again 28 after the 9.
Careful now. Is 28 our answer?

ask.ifNot: 28 is how far apart the shared numbers are. The number itself is 9 plus 28.

beats.say: 28 is the distance, not the number. 9 plus 28 is 37.
Let's check by writing them out. A carries on 21, 25, 29, 33, 37. B carries on 30, then 37. Both reach 37.
Two patterns meet again after a distance that both step sizes can make. Find that distance, then add it to the number they share.
A pattern goes up by the same amount each time. Its 5th number is 23 and its 8th number is 35. We want the 1st number.

beats.say: Each even number is double its place number. So the 19th one is 19 times 2, which is 38.
Now pair the ends. 2 and 38 make 40. 4 and 36 make 40. Every pair makes 40.
Here is the tricky part. 19 is an odd number. What happens when we pair up 19 numbers?

ask.ifNot: Pairs use the numbers 2 at a time. 9 pairs use all but one of the 19, so 1 number is left in the middle.

beats.say: 9 pairs use 18 numbers, and 1 is left alone in the middle. The middle one is the 10th even number, which is 20.
9 pairs of 40 make 360.
Don't forget the one in the middle. 360 plus 20 is 380. So the sum is 380.
A quick check. Each pair of 40 is like two 20s. So the whole sum is like 19 twenties, and 19 times 20 is 380.
When you pair up an odd count of numbers, one is left in the middle. Add it on at the end.
Look at these numbers. 1, 3, 9, 27. They grow fast! One more is hiding at the end.
Let's try the jumps first. They are 2, then 6, then 18. The jump keeps changing, so this is not a plain adding pattern.
When adding does not fit, try times. Which of these rules works at every step?

ask.ifNot: Adding 2 works for the first step, but not for the next one. Multiplying works every time: 1 times 3 is 3, and 3 times 3 is 9.

beats.say: 1 times 3 is 3. 3 times 3 is 9. 9 times 3 is 27. Each number is 3 times the one before.
So we multiply the last number by 3. 27 times 3 is 81. The next number is 81.
Let's check by going backwards. 81 divided by 3 takes us back to 27. It fits.
Keep this in mind. If adding does not fit a pattern, test times. Find the multiplier, then use it on the last number.
The series is 48, 51, 57, 69, and then a star. We must find the number hiding behind the star.

spec.note: How big is each jump? What comes next?

beats.say: Find the jumps. 51 minus 48 is 3. 57 minus 51 is 6. 69 minus 57 is 12.
The jumps are 3, 6 and 12. How do they grow?

choices: each is double the one before
ask.ifNot: 3 to 6 could be adding 3. But 6 to 12 is not adding 3. Doubling fits both: double 3 is 6, and double 6 is 12.

beats.say: The jumps double each time. So the next jump is double 12, which is 24. The trap is to use an old jump again.
69 plus 24 is 93. So the star stands for 93.
Read the jumps once more: 3, 6, 12, 24. Each one is double the last. It fits.
When the jumps are not steady, check whether they grow by adding or by multiplying. Here they doubled.
A man walks 66 kilometres in 6 days. Each day he walks 4 kilometres less than the day before. How far does he walk on the 6th day?

board.text: 66 km in 6 days. Each day 4 km less.

beats.say: We don't know how far he walked on any single day. So here is the plan: compare every day with day 6, the shortest walk of all.
Day 5 is 4 kilometres more than day 6. So how much more than day 6 is day 4?

ask.ifNot: Day 4 is 4 more than day 5, and day 5 is 4 more than day 6. That is 4 and 4, which makes 8.

beats.say: So day 5 is 4 more than day 6. Day 4 is 8 more. Then 12 more, 16 more, and day 1 is 20 more.

spec.note: Every day compared with day 6

beats.say: Add up all the extra: 4 plus 8 plus 12 plus 16 plus 20. That is 60 kilometres of extra walking.
Now take that extra 60 away from the total. What does the leftover stand for?

ask.ifNot: Without the extras, every one of the 6 days is as short as day 6. So what is left is 6 equal walks.

beats.say: 66 take away 60 leaves 6 kilometres. That is 6 equal walks, so each one is 1 kilometre.
So on the 6th day he walked just 1 kilometre.
Check. The six days were 21, 17, 13, 9, 5 and 1 kilometres. Add them up and you get 66. It works.
The trap is to share 66 equally among 6 days. The days are not equal! Compare every day with the one you want, then take away the extras.
Here is a long list: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, all the way up to 113. How many numbers are in it? Let's count without writing them all.
First the jump. 8 minus 1 is 7, and 15 minus 8 is 7 too. Each term is 7 more than the one before.
How far is it from the first term to the last? 113 minus 1 is 112.
That distance of 112 is covered in jumps of 7. How do we find the number of jumps?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 7s fit into 112. That is a division.

beats.say: Split 112 into 70 and 42. 70 divided by 7 is 10. 42 divided by 7 is 6. So there are 16 jumps.
There are 16 jumps. So how many terms are there?

ask.ifNot: Think small. 1 jump joins 2 numbers. 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: Here is the trap. Jumps sit between the terms, and the first term is there before any jump. So we add 1.
Check with the start of the list. From 1 to 29 is 4 jumps, and there are 5 terms. One more than the jumps. So there are 17 terms in all.
So the plan is: last take away first, divide by the jump to count the jumps, and add 1 to count the terms.
Here is a series: 24, 39, 53, 66, 78, and on it goes. Which number will be 10th? Let's find the rule first.
Look at the jumps between neighbours. They are 15, then 14, then 13, then 12.
The jumps are not the same. So what is happening to them?

ask.ifNot: Read the jumps again: 15, 14, 13, 12. Each one is 1 less than the one before.

beats.say: So the next jumps are 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. Count carefully: 78 is the 5th term, so we need 5 more jumps to reach the 10th.
The 6th term is 78 plus 11, which is 89. The 7th is 89 plus 10, which is 99.
The 8th is 99 plus 9, which is 108. Don't stop there! The 9th is 108 plus 8, which is 116.
One jump is left. Which jump takes us from the 9th term to the 10th?

ask.ifNot: The jumps we listed were 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. We have used four of them, so the last one is 7.

beats.say: 116 plus 7 is 123. So the 10th term is 123.
So the plan is: find the pattern in the jumps, then step forward, naming each term as you go, until you reach the one you want.
The series is 519, 398, 277, 156, and then a star. The numbers are shrinking. Let's find the next one.

spec.note: How big is each jump? What comes next?

beats.say: Find the first drop. 519 minus 398 is 121.
Before we trust that, what should we do?

ask.ifNot: One drop does not make a rule. Test the other neighbours to see if the drop is always 121.

beats.say: 398 minus 277 is 121. 277 minus 156 is 121. The drop is 121 every time.
So take 121 away from 156. Take away 100 first to get 56. Then take away 21 to get 35.
So the star stands for 35.
Check by adding back. 35 plus 121 is 156. It fits.
Find the jump, check it on every pair, then make one more jump. And with big numbers, subtract in easy pieces.
The series is 5, 14, 25, 38, then a star, then 70 and 89. This time the hidden number is in the middle.
Find the jumps we can see. 5 to 14 is 9. 14 to 25 is 11. 25 to 38 is 13.
The jumps are 9, 11, 13. What is the next jump?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 2 more than the one before. After 13 comes 15.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 2, so the next one is 15. And 38 plus 15 is 53.
Here is the good part. The numbers after the star let us check. The next jumps should be 17 and 19.
53 plus 17 is 70. And 70 plus 19 is 89. Both match the series!
So the star stands for 53.
A number in the middle has to fit on both sides. Always test your answer against the numbers that come after it.
The numbers are 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. Which number comes next?

spec.note: How big is each jump? What comes next?

beats.say: Measure the jumps. 2 to 6 is 4. 6 to 12 is 6. 12 to 20 is 8. 20 to 30 is 10.
The jumps are 4, 6, 8, 10. What will the next jump be?

ask.ifNot: The jumps go up by 2 each time: 4, 6, 8, 10. So the next jump is 12.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 2 each time. So the next jump is 12, not 10 again.
30 plus 12 is 42. So the next number is 42.
Here is another way to see these numbers. 2 is 1 times 2. 6 is 2 times 3. 12 is 3 times 4. So the 6th number is 6 times 7, which is 42 again.
When the jumps change, look for the pattern in the jumps. And if you can find a second way, use it to check.
What an odd list! Every number is just one digit, repeated. And one of the numbers has gone missing from the middle.
Don't try to subtract these giants. Look at which digit each one uses: 9, then 7, then the gap, then 3, then 1.
So which digit does the missing term use?

ask.ifNot: The digits go down by 2 each time: 9, 7, then 5, then 3, then 1.

beats.say: The digit is 5. Now count how many times each digit is written. Seven 9s. Six 7s. Then the gap. Then four 3s and three 1s.
So how many 5s does the missing term have?

ask.ifNot: The lengths go 7, 6, then the gap, then 4, 3. They go down by 1 each time, so the gap has 5 digits.

beats.say: The digit is 5 and it is written 5 times. So the missing term is five 5s in a row.
Two things had to be right at once: the digit and the length. Four 5s or six 5s would have the right digit, but not the right length.
So with odd-looking numbers, ask how each one is built. Here it was the digit used, and how many times.
The sequence is 416, 525, 636, 749. What comes next? Let's measure the jumps.
525 minus 416 is 109. 636 minus 525 is 111. 749 minus 636 is 113.
Here is the thing to spot. Are the jumps all the same?

ask.ifNot: Look closely: 109, 111, 113. Each jump is 2 more than the one before.

beats.say: The jumps look alike, but they are not the same. They grow by 2. So the next jump is 115.
749 plus 115. Add 100 to get 849. Then add 15 to get 864.
So the next term is 864.
There is a second way to see it. The first digits go 4, 5, 6, 7. And the last two digits are 4 times 4, 5 times 5, 6 times 6, 7 times 7.
So next comes 8, followed by 8 times 8, which is 64. That makes 864 again. Two ways, one answer.
Jumps that look nearly the same may still be changing. Work each one out exactly before you decide on the rule.
The list is 2, 6, 12, 20, a question mark, 42, 56. The missing number sits in the middle.
Start with the jumps we can see. 2 to 6 is 4. 6 to 12 is 6. 12 to 20 is 8.
The jumps are 4, 6, 8. So what is the jump into the missing number?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 2 bigger than the last. After 8 comes 10.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 2, so the next jump is 10. And 20 plus 10 is 30.
Now test it with the numbers after the gap. The next jumps should be 12 and 14.
30 plus 12 is 42. And 42 plus 14 is 56. Both fit the list perfectly.
So the missing number is 30.
When the gap is in the middle, the numbers after it are a free check. Use them!
Here is the sequence: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125. Each number is much bigger than the last. Let's find the next one.
Try the jumps first: 7, then 19, then 37, then 61. No easy pattern there. So let's look at each number on its own.
Think about the 8. Which of these makes 8?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 2 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. So 8 is 2 used three times in a multiplication.

beats.say: 1 times 1 times 1 is 1. 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. 3 times 3 times 3 is 27. Each counting number is used three times.
It carries on. 4 times 4 times 4 is 64, and 5 times 5 times 5 is 125.
So what do we work out for the next term?

ask.ifNot: The numbers used so far are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Next is 6, and it is used three times: 6 times 6 times 6.

beats.say: Careful: 6 times 6 is 36, but we are not done. That is only two 6s. Now 36 times 6: 30 sixes are 180, and 6 sixes are 36.
180 plus 36 is 216. So the next number is 216.
So when the jumps give no clue, look at how each number is built. These are the cube numbers: a number used three times.
Here are five terms: 53, 56, 62, 71, 83. Two more are missing at the end. Let's find them both.
Measure the jumps. 53 to 56 is 3. 56 to 62 is 6. Then 9, then 12.
The jumps are 3, 6, 9, 12. What will the next two jumps be?

ask.ifNot: 3, 6, 9, 12 are the multiples of 3. The jump grows by 3 every time, so next come 15 and then 18.

beats.say: The jumps go up by 3 each time. So the next two are 15 and 18. The trap is to use 15 twice.
83 plus 15 is 98. That is the first new term.
Now the jump grows again. 98 plus 18 is 116. That is the second new term.
So the next two terms are 98 and 116.
So: find the jumps, see how the jumps grow, and let them keep growing for each new term you add.
Here are the numbers: 525, 438, a gap, 264, 177, 90. Let's find the one that fell out.

spec.note: How big are the jumps? Find the missing number

beats.say: The numbers are going down. Find the drop from 525 to 438. 525 minus 438 is 87.
One pair is not enough to be sure of the rule. Which other pair can we use to check the drop?

ask.ifNot: We need two numbers that are next-door neighbours, with no gap between them. 264 and 177 are neighbours.

beats.say: 264 minus 177 is 87. And 177 minus 90 is 87 again. So every drop is 87.
Now take 87 away from 438. Take away 80 first to get 358. Then take away 7 to get 351.
So the missing number is 351.
Does the drop after the gap fit too? 351 take away 87 is 264. Yes, that is the very next number in the list.
So when a number is missing in the middle, use the neighbours you can see to find the jump, and test your answer on both sides.
The series is 37, 39, 42, 47, 54, then a hidden number, then 78.
Find the jumps. 37 to 39 is 2. Then 3, then 5, then 7.
The jumps are 2, 3, 5, 7. Think about which family these numbers belong to. What comes next?

ask.ifNot: If these were the odd numbers, 2 would not be there. 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime numbers. 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime. The next prime is 11.

beats.say: This is the trap. 2, 3, 5, 7 look as if 9 should follow. But they are the primes, and 9 is 3 times 3. So the next jump is 11.
54 plus 11 is 65.
Now test it with the last number. The prime after 11 is 13, and 65 plus 13 is 78. That is exactly the last number in the series.
So the hidden number is 65.
And if we had used 9? 54 plus 9 is 63. Then we would need a jump of 15 to reach 78, and that fits no pattern.
When jumps look almost like a pattern you know, check carefully which family they really belong to. Then test with the numbers that follow.
The sequence starts 53, 60, 68, 77. We want the 10th term, so first we need the rule.
Look at the jumps. 53 to 60 is 7. 60 to 68 is 8. 68 to 77 is 9.
How do the jumps change?

ask.ifNot: Read them again: 7, 8, 9. Each jump is 1 more than the one before.

beats.say: 77 is the 4th term. To reach the 10th we need 6 more jumps: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Counting them is the tricky part.
The 5th term is 77 plus 10, which is 87. The 6th is 87 plus 11, which is 98.
The 7th is 98 plus 12, which is 110. The 8th is 110 plus 13, which is 123. Don't stop there, it is only the 8th!
The 9th term is 123 plus 14, which is 137.
One jump is left. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We listed six jumps: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Five are used, so the last is 15.

beats.say: 137 plus 15 is 152. So the 10th term is 152.
When jumps keep changing, walk forward one term at a time and label each term. That way you stop at exactly the right one.
Here are five terms: 4, 7, 11, 18, 29. Two more belong at the end. Let's find them.
Try the jumps: 3, then 4, then 7, then 11. They don't grow in a steady way. So the jumps are not the key here.
Here is the idea that unlocks it. Look at 4, 7 and 11. How can you make 11 from the two numbers before it?

ask.ifNot: Just add the two numbers before it. 4 plus 7 is 11.

beats.say: 4 plus 7 is 11. 7 plus 11 is 18. 11 plus 18 is 29. Each term is the sum of the two terms before it.
So the next term is the last two added together. 18 plus 29 is 47.
Now for the second new term. Which two numbers do we add this time?

ask.ifNot: Always the two newest terms. Now those are 29 and 47.

beats.say: Careful: use the two newest terms. 29 plus 47 is 76.
So the next two terms are 47 and 76.
So if the jumps look messy, test whether each term is made from the two before it. That was the secret here.
Our terms are fractions: 1 fifth, 2 fifths, 4 fifths, 7 fifths, 11 fifths. We want the next one.
Every fraction has the same bottom number, 5. So where is the pattern hiding?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number never changes. Only the top numbers move: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11.

beats.say: Look only at the tops: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11. The jumps between them are 1, 2, 3 and 4.
So what is the next jump?

ask.ifNot: The jumps go 1, 2, 3, 4. Each is 1 more than the last, so the next is 5.

beats.say: 11 plus 5 is 16. So the next term is 16 fifths.
The choices are mixed numbers, so let's change it. 5 fifths make 1 whole. So 15 fifths make 3 wholes, and 1 fifth is left over.
So the next term is 3 and 1 fifth.
Careful: 11 fifths is the same as 2 and 1 fifth. That is the last term we were given, not the next one.
With fractions that share a bottom number, find the pattern in the tops. Then write the answer in the form the question wants.
The series is 0.25, 0.50, 1, 1.75, a hidden number, and then 4. Decimals this time, but the idea is the same.
Find the jumps. 0.50 minus 0.25 is 0.25. 1 minus 0.50 is 0.50. 1.75 minus 1 is 0.75.
The jumps are 0.25, 0.50, 0.75. What is the next jump?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 0.25 more than the last. And 0.75 plus 0.25 makes exactly 1 whole.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 0.25 each time. 0.75 plus 0.25 is 1 whole. So the next jump is 1.
Test it with the last number. The jump after 1 is 1.25. And 2.75 plus 1.25 is 4. It matches!
So the hidden number is 2.75.
Decimals follow the same plan as whole numbers. Find the jumps, see how they change, and check with the numbers that follow.
Our terms are 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. Let's find the one that comes next.
Start with the first two. How big is the jump from 3 to 7?

ask.ifNot: Count on from 3: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4 steps. Or 7 take away 3 is 4.

beats.say: 7 minus 3 is 4. Now check the others. 11 minus 7 is 4, and 15 minus 11 is 4. Every jump is 4.

spec.note: Every jump is the same size

beats.say: So the rule is: add 4 each time.
The last term is 19. 19 plus 4 is 23. So the next term is 23.
Quick check. From 19 to 23 is a jump of 4, the same as all the others. It fits.
Find the jump, check that it never changes, then add it once more. That is the whole plan.
The numbers are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. What comes next?
Try the jumps: 3, then 6, then 12, then 24. They are not steady. But look, the jumps are growing just like the numbers themselves.
So adding is not the rule. Which move works at every step?

ask.ifNot: Adding 3 works only once. Doubling works every time: double 3 is 6, and double 6 is 12.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. 6 times 2 is 12. 12 times 2 is 24. 24 times 2 is 48. Each number is double the one before.
So we double 48. Double 40 is 80, and double 8 is 16. Together that makes 96.
The trap is to add the last jump, 24, once more. But the jumps double too. The next jump is 48, and 48 plus 48 is 96.
When the jumps keep growing fast, test for multiplying. Here each number is double the one before.
The numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Let's work out what comes next.
Let's look at how each number is made. 4 is 2 times 2. 9 is 3 times 3.
So how is 16 made?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 4 is 16. Each number in the list is a counting number multiplied by itself.

beats.say: And 1 is 1 times 1, 16 is 4 times 4, and 25 is 5 times 5. These are called the square numbers.
We have used 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Next comes 6, multiplied by itself. Careful: not 5 times 6. 6 times 6 is 36.
Check with the jumps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They grow by 2, so the next jump is 11. And 25 plus 11 is 36. The same answer.
So the next number is 36. When you see 1, 4, 9, 16, think square numbers: each counting number times itself.
The numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21. What comes next?
Measure the jumps. 1 to 3 is 2. 3 to 6 is 3. Then 4, then 5, then 6.
The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. What will the next jump be?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 1 more than the one before. After 6 comes 7.

beats.say: The jump grows by 1 every time. So the next jump is 7, not 6 again.
21 plus 7 is 28. So the next number is 28.
These numbers have a nice secret. 3 is 1 plus 2. 6 is 1 plus 2 plus 3. 10 is 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4. Each one adds the next counting number.
When the jumps are not the same, look at the jumps themselves. Here they simply count up: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
The terms are 2, 5, 14, 41. Only four of them, and they grow fast. Let's find the next.
Find the jumps. 5 minus 2 is 3. 14 minus 5 is 9. 41 minus 14 is 27.
The jumps are 3, 9 and 27. How do they grow?

ask.ifNot: 3 to 9 could be adding 6. But 9 plus 6 is not 27. Times 3 fits both: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27.

beats.say: This is the thing to spot. The jumps don't grow by adding. Each jump is 3 times the one before. So the next jump is 27 times 3, which is 81.
41 plus 81 is 122. So the next term is 122.
Here is a second way to see it. Each term is 3 times the one before, take away 1. 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 take away 1 is 5.
Try it on the last term. 41 times 3 is 123, and 123 take away 1 is 122. Both ways agree.
When the jumps are not steady, ask if they are multiplied each time. And a second way to the same answer is the best check.
The terms are 1, 2, 6, 24, 120. They grow faster and faster. What is next?
Adding can't keep up with growth like this, so think times. 1 times 2 is 2. 2 times 3 is 6.
Now from 6 to 24. 6 times what makes 24?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 4 is 24. We are multiplying here, not adding.

beats.say: 6 times 4 is 24, and 24 times 5 is 120. Look at the multipliers: 2, 3, 4, 5.
So what do we multiply by next?

ask.ifNot: The multiplier goes up by 1 each time: 2, 3, 4, 5. So the next one is 6.

beats.say: 120 times 6. 100 sixes are 600 and 20 sixes are 120. Together that is 720.
So the next term is 720. The trap is to use an old multiplier again. Here the multiplier itself keeps growing.
In some patterns you multiply by a different number each time. Then look for the pattern in the multipliers.
The numbers are 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. One more belongs at the end.
Try the jumps: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. That is strange. The jumps look just like the list itself, one step behind!
That is a big clue. Look at 2, 3 and 5. How is 5 made from the two numbers before it?

ask.ifNot: Add the two numbers just before it. 2 plus 3 is 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. 3 plus 5 is 8. 5 plus 8 is 13. 8 plus 13 is 21. Each number is the sum of the two before it.
So add the last two numbers in the list, 13 and 21. Careful: use both of them, not 21 and an old jump.
13 plus 21 is 34. So the missing number is 34.
This is a famous pattern. When the jumps look odd, test whether each number is the two before it added together.
Here are six numbers: 2, 5, 10, 17, 28, 37. Five follow a rule and one does not. Let's catch it.

spec.note: One number breaks the pattern. Look at the jumps

beats.say: Measure the jumps. They are 3, then 5, then 7, then 11, then 9.
Most of those jumps go up nicely. Which two look out of order?

ask.ifNot: 3, 5, 7 go up by 2 each time. Next should come 9 and then 11. But here they come as 11 and then 9.

beats.say: Both of those jumps touch 28. The jump into 28 is too big, and the jump out of it is too small. So 28 is the one that breaks the pattern.
What should be there instead? 17 plus 9 is 26. And then 26 plus 11 is 37, which matches the last number.
Here is another way to see it. Each number is a square number plus 1. 1 times 1 plus 1 is 2. 2 times 2 plus 1 is 5. 3 times 3 plus 1 is 10.
Then 5 times 5 plus 1 is 26, not 28. So the number that does not belong is 28.
To find the odd one out, look at the jumps. The number sitting between two jumps that don't fit is the culprit.
The terms are 4, 12, 36, 108. Let's find the next term.
From 4 to 12 we could add 8, or we could multiply by 3. Which of these also works from 12 to 36?

ask.ifNot: Adding 8 to 12 does not give 36. But 12 times 3 is 36. So the rule is times 3.

beats.say: 4 times 3 is 12. 12 times 3 is 36. 36 times 3 is 108. Each term is 3 times the one before.
So the next term is 108 times 3. 100 threes are 300, and 8 threes are 24.
300 plus 24 is 324. So the next term is 324.
Check by going backwards. 324 divided by 3 is 108. It fits.
One step can fool you, because adding and multiplying may both fit it. Always test your rule on a second step.
This time we are given the rule: n times, n plus 1. Here n is the place of the term: 1 for the 1st, 2 for the 2nd, and so on.
Let's test the rule. The 1st term is 1 times 2. The 2nd is 2 times 3. The 3rd is 3 times 4. Each is the place number times the number just after it.
So for the 10th term, which two numbers do we multiply?

ask.ifNot: Here n is 10. And n plus 1 is the number just after it, which is 11.

beats.say: n is 10, and the number just after it is 11. Careful: 9 times 10 would be the 9th term, not the 10th.
10 times 11 is 110. So the 10th term is 110.
Check the rule on the last term we can see. The 6th term should be 6 times 7, which is 42. Yes, it matches.
When a rule uses n, put the place number in for n. Then you can jump straight to any term without listing them all.
The numbers are 729, 243, 81, 27, 9. They shrink quickly. What comes next?
Look at the small end, where the numbers are easy. Which rule works at every step?

ask.ifNot: 27 take away 18 is 9, but 81 take away 18 is not 27. Dividing by 3 works every time.

beats.say: 27 divided by 3 is 9. 81 divided by 3 is 27. 243 divided by 3 is 81. Each number is the one before it, divided by 3.
So divide the last number by 3. 9 divided by 3 is 3.
The trap is to subtract. 9 take away 3 is 6, but this pattern divides. It never takes away.
Check by going back up. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27. It fits.
So the next number is 3. When numbers shrink fast, test for dividing, and start with the small numbers where it is easy to see.
What a tangle: 1, 1, 2, 4, 3, 9, 4, 16, 5, and then a gap. It goes up and down, so one simple rule won't do.
Read every second number, starting from the very first. What do you get?

ask.ifNot: Start at the first number and skip one each time: 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, then 5.

beats.say: Two patterns are woven together. One is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The numbers in between are 1, 4, 9, 16.
Look at each pair. 2 is followed by 4. 3 is followed by 9. 4 is followed by 16. Each in-between number is the number before it, times itself.
The gap comes straight after the 5. So what goes there?

ask.ifNot: The gap belongs to the in-between pattern. It is the number just before it, times itself. That is 5 times 5.

beats.say: The gap is not the next counting number. It belongs to the in-between pattern. 5 times 5 is 25.
So the next term is 25. When a list zigzags, split it into two patterns, and work out which one the gap belongs to.
